In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple took a step forward in its long-standing ambition to make the iPhone feel like a single piece of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display.

Achieving this without letting the Face ID components show through the display or compromising display quality in that area requires fairly ingenious engineering…

Jony Ive once described his long-term vision for the iPhone as a single slab of glass, and although he has left the company, that goal has endured. Apple ultimately hopes to embed all of the technology that currently takes up screen real estate beneath the display, including Face ID and the front-facing camera.

The iPhone 18 Pro is the first to achieve this step, but it certainly wasn't easy. Face ID requires the TrueDepth module to emit and receive infrared light — and infrared light cannot pass through display pixels.

Apple had to create sufficiently large gaps between the pixels to let the infrared light pass through, without any visible impact on the display. To do so, the company's engineers set about designing an entirely new pixel arrangement that increases the gaps without affecting what the pixels display.

iFixit demonstrated this pixel arrangement under a microscope, and Apple also confirmed to me that the overall pixel density is reduced by half across the entire module area. This could have created a second problem: halving the pixel density would likely make that region of the display noticeably dimmer, so Apple boosted the brightness of those pixels to compensate. In addition, the components appear to have been fitted with an infrared filter to block visible light from passing through the gaps, further concealing the parts beneath.

The results are pretty astonishing. In real-world conditions, you can't see the TrueDepth camera components even if you look really, really closely. I tried macro photography with a variety of display colours and lighting conditions and still couldn't capture it. That said, iFixit's microscopic images can still detect it, but you absolutely wouldn't notice it in everyday use.

This technology currently allows the Dynamic Island to shrink, in turn supporting three Live Activities at once instead of two. In some future iPhone model, the front-facing camera will also be hidden under the display. This is already technically possible today, but the image quality trade-offs remain beyond what Apple is willing to accept. It's only a matter of time before that problem is solved.
